messages.author: 8da5b06c56385794
messages.subject: Numeric overflow
parts:
Hi everyone.

I've been wrestling with this issue for a couple days now and I'm pretty much out of ideas. I'm using Pystan to fit a model (model string and dat attached). Python version is 3.3.3. 64bit Linux, Kernel 3.12.3-1-ARCH, 8GB memory. gcc is version 4.8.2 and I believe that's what Stan is using (I've seen gcc errors before).

I'm getting a numeric overflow exception when trying to fit a model with 3 chains and 10000 saved steps. The model is fairly simple and the data seems valid, so I'm not really sure what's going on. The model is being fit in a big loop - I'm fitting on the order of 100 models in a long batch job. The exception occurs non-deterministically in this loop, no doubt due to the Monte Carlo nature of the sampler.

Is it reasonable to call a model valid if I continually re-fit until the exception doesn't occur, or should I be changing the model so that it does not numerically overflow 100% of the time. Is there a clear reason why I'm seeing this behaviour?

Thanks for any help.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Numeric overflow
parts:
Are you just seeing a warning or is exception causing the code to die? Numerical overflow
should lead to rejected samples, which is fine statistically if inefficient.

For best performance, however, try to make your model more well-posed. Try tighter priors
or reparameterizing so that the bulk of the posterior mass is within a reasonable range.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Numeric overflow
parts:
I'm surprised you're getting overflow given the fairly dispersed
data you have. Even some mild priors on alpha and beta should
solve the problem, though --- you're using an improper prior that's
uniform on (0,inf). Gelman et al. discuss priors for beta distributions
in chapter 5 and reparameterize in terms of mean alpha/(alpha + beta)
and total count (alpha + beta) --- we use that as an example in the
reparameterization chapter of the manul.

Unfortunately for this model choice, your data don't look like they come from
a beta distribution --- the data looks multimodal concentrated around .99
and .36 (with all the values around 0.36 apparently identical).
So a simple beta distribution won't be very good for this
data, even when you get the model to fit. So I'm guessing the model runs
off to fit one of the modes really well.

I'd also suggest a constraint on the data variables N and y, because your
model requires N >= 0 and 0 < y[n] < 1. It won't change behavior,
only help with error checking.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Numeric overflow
parts:
That's a bug in PyStan. I'm not sure if it originates in
Stan or not. I'd run your models and see, but I don't know
how to handle the JSON-formatted data.

What should happen is that the error should be caught and the sample
rejected. You still might not be able to fit the model, but
an overflow in digamma() shouldn't cause the sampler to die.

However we fix Stan, you need a better model. The
computational problem is a symptom of a problem in the model ---
what Andrew calls the "folk theorem". In this case, there are
two issues with the model: (a) no priors on the parameters to
the beta distribution, and (b) the beta distribution doesn't fit
the data. With a prior, you should be able to get a (bad)
fit computationally.

- Bob

On 1/1/14, 9:31 PM, Filip Krynicki wrote:
> Thanks for all the help, the response has been well beyond what I could have hoped.

We take bugs seriously, and diagnosing them often involves
us having to dive into the particulars of the models.

We're also interested in bringing more people up to speed in
Bayesian modeling and want to understand where new users have
problems.

> I have a very naive question. How
> would I specify a prior on the alpha and beta parameters? My understanding is that the lower and upper keywords specify
> hard constraints (or as close as is allowed given numerical precision issues).

They restrict alpha and beta to the constrained ranges (both > 0 in this case,
modulo arithmetic underflow, which can make them 0). Then you get a uniform
prior over that range, which is improper in this case because

INTEGRAL_0^infinity const dx = infinity

> Do I specify a prior by sampling the
> alpha and beta parameters from a distribution defined by a hyperparameter?

Yes, but the sampling statements don't actually do sampling. So
you don't actually sample alpha and beta from their priors, per se,
though that's the generative story of your model. In Stan, sampling
statements just add terms to the log probability function.
> I'm looking through the manual for any mention of priors and coming up with nothing.

They're all over the place in the manual. In the
very first example there's a beta prior on theta.

We're assuming a fair degree of background in Bayesian
stats, though there's a chapter near the end of the manual
on Bayesian data analysis that recapitulates the initial
chapter(s) of Gelman et al.'s book of the same name.

> My thinking would be (using a
> normal prior for both parameters for simplicity's sake):
>
> data {
> ...
> real prior_mu;
> real prior_sigma;
> }
>
> parameters {
> real alpha;
> real beta;
> }
>
> model {
> alpha ~ normal(prior_mu, prior_sigma)
> beta ~ normal(prior_mu, prior_sigma)
> for (i in 1:N) {
> y[i] ~ beta(alpha, beta);
> }
> }
>
> This model compiles and runs but I have little confidence that it's doing what I think it is from a theoretical standpoint.

This is OK, theoretically at least. The prior is
technically a normal truncated to the constrained values.

A more typical prior might be an exponential or lognormal, if you
put it direclty on alpha and beta. But it's more typical to do
what we discuss in section 17.1 of the manual, which specifically discusses
priors for the beta distribution in terms of a reparameterization
in terms of the mean (alpha / (alpha + beta)) and
total prior count (alpha + beta). There we use a Pareto prior following
Gelman et al.'s Bayesian Data Analysis, but a lognormal or
exponential (or more geneally gamma) would also make sense.

- Bob
